title: She follows her mother with ungainly steps, a mare leading her fillyfoal. Twilight phantoms are they, yet moulded in prophetic grace of structure, slim shapely haunches, a supple tendonous neck, the meek apprehensive skull.
html_source: This is how Bloom would compare his daughter Milly to her mother. Carol Loeb Schloss, in Lucia Joyce: To Dance in the Wake, however, asserts that Joyce thinks of Milly as “that once coveted, but impossible-to-possess student lover of days gone by. To herself she is ‘silly Milly’ [from Calypso episode], but to her father she is "Millicent, the young, the dear, the radiant [see next paragraph], who ‘follows her mother with ungainly steps, a mare leading her fillyfoal. Twilight phantoms are they yet moulded in prophetic grace and structure, … etc.’ From the mother Molly to the daughter Milly, from the mother mare to the daughter filly, the girl child in Ulysses is perceived to be a smaller, newer version of the older woman. This is so whether that woman is considered to be her actual mother or her more spiritually similar progenitor, the mystery lady from Trieste who gave her a flower. She is ‘the same thing [as her precursor] watered down,’ [from Hades episode] as if all women, in time, shared the same biological fate. ‘Destiny’ thinks Bloom. [from Calypso episode]. The pronoun "she” at the beginning of this passage references back to the “soul,” and in that context perhaps the message is that it is that entity that is affected in its “grace,” “shapeliness,” “suppleness,” and “meek apprehensiveness” by its precursors. Perhaps this is as true for Stephen as it is for Milly.
